analysis.one_liner: Extends unpaid family and medical leave and equal-treatment protections to part-time and temporary workers.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Elizabeth Warren with 8 cosponsors, was referred to the Senate labor committee in September 2023 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make part-time and short-tenure workers eligible for unpaid, job-protected family and medical leave under the Family and Medical Leave Act, which today requires a year on the job and 1,250 hours worked. It would also bar employers from paying part-time workers less, giving them fewer benefits, or offering them worse schedules than full-time workers doing the same jobs. Employers would have to offer extra hours to current employees who want them before hiring new staff or temp workers, and pay existing workers for hours a new hire works during time the employee had asked to work.
analysis.who_benefits: Part-time and temporary workers — in retail, food service, care work, and other hourly jobs — gain access to family and medical leave after 90 days instead of being excluded, and gain the right to equal pay, pro rata benefits, promotion consideration, and advance input into their schedules. Existing employees who want more hours would get first call on them before the employer hires outsiders or temp-agency staff. The protections also cover federal employees, congressional staff, and state employees, and apply to franchise chains counted together rather than store by store.

how_it_helps.text: Part-time workers and people in their first year on the job would become eligible for unpaid, job-protected family and medical leave after 90 days of employment, replacing the current requirement of 12 months of service plus at least 1,250 hours in the prior year, with matching changes for federal, congressional, and state employees.

The bill makes it illegal for an employer to pay a part-time worker less, deny them pro rata paid and unpaid time off and other benefits, or withhold promotions and input into schedules when their job requires substantially equal skill, effort, and responsibility under similar conditions.

When hiring, employers must record each worker's desired weekly hours and availability, and must offer available hours to existing employees before hiring anyone new, including through a temp or staffing agency; if a new hire or contractor works during hours an existing employee had asked for, the employer must compensate the existing worker for that hour, subject to exceptions for overtime, qualifications, and unavailability.

Workers could enforce these rights in court, recovering lost wages and benefits plus an equal amount in liquidated damages and attorney's fees, with the Labor Department empowered to investigate, subpoena records, and fine employers $500 to $5,000 per willful violation, adjusted for inflation.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with more than 15 employees — counted across whole franchise chains and staffing networks — bear the cost: raising part-time pay and benefits to match full-time peers, tracking each worker's desired hours and scheduling them first, paying existing workers for hours new hires take during requested time, and keeping three years of compliance records for Labor Department inspection. Temporary staffing agencies lose placements because employers can no longer use them to fill hours current employees want.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large part-time employers and staffing agencies

drawbacks.text: The requirement to compensate existing employees for hours worked by new hires during time they had asked to work adds a new payroll cost, which could make employers more cautious about taking on additional part-time staff or expanding hours at all.

Counting an entire franchise chain or network of businesses as one employer for the 15-employee threshold pulls small individual franchisees, who may have only a handful of workers on site, into the full recordkeeping, scheduling, and equal-treatment obligations.

The offer-hours-first rule and the pay requirement limit how employers can use staffing agencies and contractors, constraining a scheduling flexibility that some businesses use to cover unpredictable demand.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly one in four American workers who are part-time, the bill addresses real exclusions: today they can be paid less for identical work, denied leave protection, and scheduled without any say. The compliance costs on employers are real but bounded — the 15-employee threshold keeps the smallest businesses out, merit and production systems are expressly allowed, and liquidated damages can be reduced for good-faith violations. The strongest honest objection is the pay-for-hours-not-worked rule, which is unusual and could discourage hiring. The bill never advanced far enough for a committee to weigh these tradeoffs in public.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate's labor committee for the rest of the Congress and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025, without ever getting a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the Part-Time Worker Bill of Rights Act in the Senate on September 19, 2023, with eight original cosponsors, all Democrats or independents.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the full action history records nothing after the referral.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired without reaching the Senate floor or the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large part-time employers — retail and restaurant chains, franchise networks, and staffing agencies — were better off because the scheduling, equal-pay, and pay-for-requested-hours requirements never took effect; part-time workers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large part-time employers and staffing firms

sides.party_line_note: All eight cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists.

industries.note: The bill bars employers from using temp agencies or contractors to fill hours that existing employees have said they want to work, and makes employers pay current workers for any such hours an outsider covers. That cuts directly into the staffing industry's core business of supplying flexible part-time labor.

industries.industry: Retail, fast food, and other large part-time employers
industries.note: These businesses would have to pay part-timers the same as full-timers doing equal work, extend pro rata benefits, give employees say over schedules, and offer hours to current staff first. Their existing model of cheaper, on-call part-time labor is what the bill targets.

The bill counts an entire franchisor network as one employer once the network exceeds 15 workers, so individual franchisees — even with a few employees — fall under the new obligations. Franchisees gain workers covered by clearer rules but bear compliance and pay costs sized to the whole brand.
